Those who do must have displayed some level of tolerance, administrative capacity and resistance to undue pressure from powerful people seeking retribution.
The same cannot be said about politicians and elected officials, who come with varying degrees of experience and tolerance but find themselves in high office.
And with the alteration of the Constitution allowing for state policing, things are about to change. Those changes could come with the good, the bad and the ugly.
When people in positions of authority cannot handle criticism or are thin-skinned, citizens usually get hurt.
The list of citizens who have been arrested, detained or harassed for insulting or making comments about state governors on social media runs into the hundreds.
While some of the commentary by Nigerians focuses on the personal failings of their governors, most centres on bad governance or insecurity.
Last year, an 18-year-old woman, Hamdiyya Sidi Sharif, was arrested and detained for criticising Governor Ahmed Aliyu of Sokoto over his handling of insecurity in the state.
Late last year, Samuel Bature was detained by the DSS for criticising Governor Caleb Mutfwang of Plateau State on social media.
And in 2022, Umar Isah, a 16-year-old boy, was arrested for insulting Governor Mai Mala Buni of Yobe State on social media. There are many more examples across the states.
Without a doubt, many young people on social media have no filters. They barely know the laws of the land and are totally oblivious to the fact that governors, too, can feel insecure.
As governors get their own private armies, freeing them from the supervision of the IGP, critics, not just criminals, need to be wary.
Governors know their own limitations. Some will need to appoint compassionate individuals to head the state police as counterweights to their worst impulses, while other governors might need police chiefs who will be firm in upholding the law.
But the best protection for citizens against the high-handedness of potential state policing and prosecutorial powers is institutionalised police departments founded on the rule of law and manned by well-trained and educated officers.
For many states, laying the right foundation in establishing their own police forces and passing the relevant laws could make or mar this nationwide experiment.
The federal government is already thinking ahead, with Femi Gbajabiamila, Chief of Staff to the President, planning a bill for a National Police Force. The states also need draft laws to be ready. In that regard, states like Lagos and Kano could end up leading the way in capacity building and creating state police forces from scratch.
But even in Kano, Governor Abba Yusuf has had cause to arrest or detain citizens critical of his administration. Amnesty International has even voiced concerns about it .
